metaDescription: Five cordless circular saws under $100 compared on blade size, cut depth, bare tool versus kit and the battery trade-offs that decide real run time.
expertTake: A cordless circular saw under $100 almost always means a bare tool or a no-name kit, and the Makita XSS02Z is the best overall because it brings a real 2-1/4 inch depth of cut and a 0 to 50 degree bevel to an 18V platform you may already own. The Yowmoft brushless kit is the best complete package for someone starting from zero. The RIDGID is the value pick for RIDGID battery owners, and the GALAX mini is for thin stock only. If you cut a lot of 2x lumber or sheet goods, buy a corded saw instead.
introParagraphs: A circular saw cuts with a spinning toothed disc, and the battery is the engine of a cordless one, which is why a saw can look cheap and still cost far more once you add a pack and charger. At a low price the real question is what you are buying: a tool, a tool and a battery, or a toy.

This guide explains what a cordless saw can and cannot do at this price, how blade size and motor type change run time, and which compromises are fine for deck repair and shelving. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below match each saw to a kind of work.

products.name: Makita XSS02Z 18V LXT 6-1/2-Inch Cordless Circular Saw, Tool Only

specList.label: Kit
specList.value: Tool only, battery and charger separate

products.description:
The XSS02Z is the saw to buy if the Makita LXT 18V platform is already on your shelf. It spins a 6-1/2 inch blade at 3,700 rpm through an electronically controlled motor, and its 2-1/4 inch depth at 90 degrees clears a 2x lumber board with margin. The machined aluminum base is the detail that matters most: a flat, stiff shoe holds the blade square to the cut, where stamped steel shoes flex and wander.

The 0 to 50 degree bevel capacity covers every common angle, including the 45 degree miters used in trim and framing. Against the DEKOPRO's 4,500 rpm, the Makita runs slower, and a lower speed with a sturdier motor is the usual recipe for cutting wet lumber without bogging down. Because it is a bare tool, the actual all-in cost depends on whether you own a battery.

The LXT platform is the long-term argument: the same battery runs Makita drills, sanders and lights. A 6-1/2 inch saw is lighter than a 7-1/4 inch and fits well in one hand, but it does not cut as deep. Replace the stock blade with a thin-kerf carbide blade if you cut plywood, since stock blades are built for general use.
products.bestFor: Makita owners and buyers who want a quality saw and plan to build a platform.
pros: Machined aluminum base keeps cuts square and flat
2-1/4 inch depth clears a 2x board
0 to 50 degree bevel covers all common angles
LXT battery fits a huge range of tools
cons: Bare tool, so battery and charger cost extra
Slower no-load speed than the budget kits
Stock blade is adequate, not smooth for plywood

products.name: Yowmoft 6-1/2-Inch Brushless Cordless Circular Saw, 20V 4Ah Kit

specList.label: Aids
specList.value: LED light, red beam guide, safety lock

products.description:
The Yowmoft is the only saw in this guide that arrives ready to cut, with a brushless motor, a 4.0 Ah battery and a charger in the box. Brushless motors switch current electronically, so they waste less energy as heat and stretch a battery further, and a 4.0 Ah pack is large for a saw at this price. That pairing means more cuts per charge than any other kit here.

A 1-3/8 inch dust port accepts a shop vacuum hose, which is a rare feature in this class and valuable if you cut indoors. The bevel runs 0 to 45 degrees, five degrees short of the Makita, which is enough for ordinary miters. The red beam guide and LED help you see the cut line, though a laser is only as accurate as its alignment.

The trade-off is a no-name brand with no deep platform behind it, so a replacement battery in three years may be hard to find. Against the DEKOPRO, which includes two 4.0 Ah packs, the Yowmoft has one pack and a brushless motor. Check the blade for run-out the first time you mount it, and set the depth to just clear the board for safer and faster cuts.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want a saw, battery and charger in one box.
pros: Brushless motor and 4.0 Ah pack stretch run time
1-3/8 inch dust port connects to a vacuum
Complete kit with charger and safety lock
LED and beam guide help line up cuts
cons: Unknown platform with uncertain spare batteries
Single pack means a wait when it drains

products.name: DEKOPRO 20V 6-1/2-Inch Cordless Circular Saw, Two 4.0Ah Batteries
products.description:
The DEKOPRO is built around a simple idea: ship two 4.0 Ah batteries so that one is always charged. For a saw, that is a bigger upgrade than any feature on a spec sheet, because a cordless circular saw draws heavy current and drains a pack quickly in thick stock. A second pack means you swap and keep cutting.

Its 4,500 rpm no-load speed is the highest here, and the listing promotes efficient cutting, though a speed number tells you little about torque. Fast blades cut cleanly in thin stock and plywood, but they bog in wet or dense lumber where a slower, stronger motor like the Makita's holds up. The listing does not say brushless, so assume a conventional motor.

What you get is a competent saw for deck repair, shed building and fence work, with enough battery to finish a morning. The body is shaped for comfort, which helps over long sessions. Treat the build claims in the listing as marketing, and inspect the base for flatness and the blade guard for smooth operation before your first cut.
products.bestFor: Weekend builders who need uninterrupted run time more than a premium platform.
pros: Two 4.0 Ah batteries mean one is always ready
4,500 rpm gives clean cuts in thin stock
Complete kit with charger
Comfortable grip for long sessions
cons: High rpm does not mean strong torque in wet lumber

products.name: RIDGID 18V Cordless 6-1/2-Inch Circular Saw, Tool Only
products.description:
The RIDGID adds the one safety feature the others lack: an electronic blade brake that stops the blade within a second or so after you release the trigger. A brake reduces the time the blade coasts and cuts accidentally, which is a real benefit for anyone cutting at a bench or on a ladder. The listings for the other saws here do not mention one, so this is the RIDGID's clearest advantage.

A heavy-duty aluminum base, like the Makita's, keeps the cut flat and resists bending when you drop the saw, and an LED lights the cut line in dim garages. It is a tool-only product, so the price depends on whether you already own an 18V RIDGID pack. If you do, it is excellent value. If not, the Yowmoft or DEKOPRO kits are cheaper overall.

Confirm the warranty terms for the tool and the battery before you rely on them. Keep the base clean of sawdust and check the blade guard spring, because a sticky guard is the commonest fault on any circular saw.
products.bestFor: RIDGID battery owners and anyone who values an electronic blade brake.
pros: Electronic blade brake stops the blade quickly
Heavy-duty aluminum base stays flat
LED helps in dark garages
Fits RIDGID 18V batteries you may already own
cons: Bare tool, battery and charger cost extra
No depth or bevel figures on the listing
Spare packs mean buying into the RIDGID line

products.name: GALAX PRO 20V Cordless Mini Circular Saw, 4-1/2 Inch, 2.0Ah
products.description:
The GALAX is a mini saw, and it is honest about it. A 4-1/2 inch blade cuts only 1-11/16 inches deep at 90 degrees, which will not complete a cut through a 2x4, and at 45 degrees the depth falls to 1-1/8 inches. It is the right tool for plywood, laminate flooring, trim and thin boards, where its small blade and light weight make controlled cuts easy.

Compared with the 6-1/2 inch saws, it gives up about 5/8 inch of depth against the Makita and a lot of battery life against the Yowmoft's 4.0 Ah. Its 2.0 Ah pack is small, so plan on cutting in bursts. The laser helps with straight lines, and the kit comes with two blades.

The small size is also its safety advantage: the blade is smaller, the saw is lighter and a beginner can control it with one hand. It is a good second saw for a workshop that already has a full-size one, or a first saw for light craft work. Do not buy it for framing.
products.bestFor: Craft, flooring and thin-stock cutting where depth matters less than control.
pros: Light and controllable for one-handed cuts
Laser guide helps straight lines in sheet stock
Two blades included in the kit
Complete 20V kit with battery
cons: 1-11/16 inch depth cannot cut through a 2x4 in one pass
Not suited to framing or deck work

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Makita and RIDGID are bare tools, while the Yowmoft, DEKOPRO and GALAX include batteries and a charger. A bare tool looks cheaper but is only a bargain if you own the matching pack. Add the cost of a 4.0 Ah battery and charger before comparing, and check that the pack is genuine. Among kits, the DEKOPRO's two 4.0 Ah packs give the most run time. If you already own an 18V Makita or RIDGID battery, the bare tool route can make the Makita or RIDGID the cheapest saw in this guide by far.

A 6-1/2 inch blade cuts about 2-1/4 inches deep at 90 degrees, as the Makita does, which is enough to cut a 2x4 in one pass. A 4-1/2 inch blade like the GALAX's cuts only 1-11/16 inches, which fails on 2x lumber. Bevel cuts reduce depth further, so check the 45 degree figure. For lumber, buy 6-1/2 inch or larger. A 6-1/2 inch saw weighs less than a 7-1/4 inch one and is easier to hold, but it will not rip thick hardwood as fast.

A brushless motor controls current electronically and wastes less energy than brushed designs, which is why the Yowmoft's brushless saw with a 4.0 Ah battery gets more cuts per charge. Circular saws are heavy loads, so efficiency matters more than in a drill. If your use is occasional, brushed is acceptable. Run time depends heavily on material, and a 4.0 Ah pack cutting thin plywood will outlast the same pack cutting wet 2x lumber by several times.

The DEKOPRO's 4,500 rpm and the GALAX's 3,400 rpm are no-load speeds. Under load, torque matters more, and the Makita's 3,700 rpm with an electronically controlled motor is built for sustained cutting. A fast blade burns and bogs in wet lumber when torque is low. Judge by motor type and platform, not rpm alone. If you cut at high speed through wet lumber, expect the blade to bind and the motor to overheat, whatever the rpm figure.

The shoe is the flat plate that rides on the board, and the Makita and RIDGID use aluminum bases. Stamped steel bases bend if dropped and drift off square. Check a base with a straightedge, and if you see a bow, return it. A square cut starts with a flat, rigid shoe. Always check that the base is flat by laying a straightedge across it, because budget bases sometimes arrive bowed.

An electronic blade brake, found on the RIDGID, stops the blade quickly after release and reduces the risk of a coasting blade. The listings for the Makita and the budget kits do not mention one. A brake is a safety feature worth paying for if you work on ladders or share the shop with others. For ladders and roof work, the blade brake reduces the coast time, which is a safety margin worth having.

specDecoder.meaning: Blade diameter sets the maximum depth of cut. A larger blade reaches deeper but weighs more. A larger blade reaches deeper, but also weighs more and demands more torque from the motor.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some mini saws claim to be circular saws but cannot cut a 2x4. The GALAX's 1-11/16 inch depth is a clear example.

specDecoder.meaning: This is blade speed with nothing to cut. It falls once the blade meets wood. Blades are rated for a maximum rpm, so confirm that the blade you fit is rated above the saw's no-load speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEKOPRO's 4,500 rpm looks big, but speed without torque burns edges.

specDecoder.meaning: Ah measures battery capacity. A 4.0 Ah pack stores twice the energy of a 2.0 Ah pack. One amp-hour is 1,000 mAh, so the 4,000 mAh packs some listings quote are 4.0 Ah.
specDecoder.watchFor: Check the Ah of every battery the kit includes, since the GALAX has 2.0 Ah and the others 4.0 Ah.

specDecoder.meaning: The angle range the shoe can tilt. Most saws bevel to 45 degrees, and the Makita reaches 50. Bevel capacity of 50 degrees lets the saw cut a 45 degree miter with margin.
specDecoder.watchFor: Depth shrinks at higher bevels, so note the 45 degree depth.

specDecoder.meaning: Brushless motors use electronic switching and no brushes. Brushless motors also tend to produce less noise and heat.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Yowmoft's listing says brushless here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cut depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared blade size and listed depth at 90 degrees, since depth decides whether a saw can cut dimensional lumber. The Makita (2-1/4 inch) set the standard. We checked listed depth at 90 degrees for each saw because that single figure decides if it can cut a 2x4.

howWeEvaluated.title: Total cost of ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed whether each saw includes a battery and charger, because the bare tool price hides the full cost. We compared packs and chargers on whether the kit included them and how large they were.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared packs: two 4.0 Ah on the DEKOPRO, one 4.0 Ah on the Yowmoft and 2.0 Ah on the GALAX. The two bare tools were ranked assuming you own a compatible battery, and we flagged the cost if you do not.

howWeEvaluated.title: Base and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We rewarded aluminum bases, brakes and bevel range, which affect accuracy and risk. We considered safety extras such as brakes and detents.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit across the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: Each saw was placed by owner type. The final order reflects what each saw is best at.

howToChoose.intro: Match the saw to what you cut.
howToChoose.note: Do not buy the mini saw for 2x lumber.
Bare tools only make sense if you own the battery.

cards.label: Tool only
cards.text: The Makita XSS02Z and RIDGID are sold without a battery. If you already own a matching pack, the price is a bargain.

cards.label: Full kit
cards.text: The Yowmoft, DEKOPRO and GALAX include batteries and chargers and cut out of the box.

howToChoose.note: Own a battery, buy the bare tool. Otherwise buy a kit.
Brushless matters most if you cut thick stock.

howToChoose.intro: Decks need depth and run time.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A 6-1/2 inch blade, at least 2 inches of depth and two batteries. A dust port helps if you cut indoors.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Makita and DEKOPRO fit best, with the Yowmoft as the brushless alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You rip lots of lumber or frame. A corded 7-1/4 inch saw or a brushless pro cordless saw is better.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You make a few cuts a month. The GALAX or Yowmoft will do.

maintenance.why: A sticky guard is dangerous. Brush out sawdust and check the spring. Wipe resin from the blade with a cleaner.
A dull blade strains the motor and battery. Use a sharp carbide blade. Check the blade bolt tightness.
A bent base cuts out of square. Check with a straightedge. Blow dust from the electronics.
Heat ages lithium cells. Avoid cars. Cycle the battery occasionally.
Blocked vents overheat the motor. Blow them out. Inspect the power cord on corded tools.

faq.q: Can a cordless circular saw replace a corded one?
faq.a: For most home work, yes. For heavy ripping and framing, a corded saw or pro cordless saw runs longer. Buy a spare blade at the same time, because the stock blade will dull before the battery does.

faq.q: What blade size should I choose?
faq.a: A 6-1/2 inch blade cuts 2x lumber. A 4-1/2 inch blade cannot. Check the voltage of the battery against the tool, since 18V and 20V MAX are the same nominal voltage but platforms do not cross over.
They can be, but check the guard action, base flatness and charger quality. Stick with included batteries only. Wait for the blade to stop before setting the saw down.

faq.q: How many cuts will a battery make?
faq.a: A 4.0 Ah pack can make dozens of cuts in thin stock, fewer in thick lumber.

faq.q: Do I need a blade brake?
faq.a: It is not required, but it reduces risk. The RIDGID has one.

faq.q: Can I cut plywood with the stock blade?
faq.a: Yes, but it may splinter. A fine-tooth plywood blade gives a cleaner edge.
